newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-court upholds Britain in sado-masochism case.
newsitem.headline: Euro-court upholds Britain in sado-masochism case.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights, in a key ruling on privacy rights, on Wednesday upheld Britain's right to jail sado-masochists for harmful sexual acts between consenting adults.

"The state was unquestionably entitled to regulate the infliction of physical harm through the criminal law. The determination of the tolerable level of harm where the victim consented was primarily a matter for the state's authorities," the court ruled.
The decision came in a 1992 case in which three British homosexuals were given prison sentences for sado-masochistic sexual acts.
The case was appealed to the European rights court by Britons Colin Laskey, who died in 1995 aged 52, Anthony Brown, 62, and Roland Jaggard, 50.
They had been given prison sentences of three to six months for belonging to a group of gays who inflicted genital injuries and whipped and branded one another during sexual orgies.
The participants were consenting adults and caused no permanent harm to each other. They used a code word during their orgies to call a halt to the infliction of pain.
They also videotaped their orgies for their own use, but some of the tapes fell into police hands.
Following their arrest and conviction on charges of causing bodily harm, among others, all three men lost their jobs and Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment.
A unanimous nine-judge chamber of the rights court said it found no basis for allegations that the British courts were biased against gays.
It upheld the authorities' decision to delve into the three men's private lives as "necessary in a democratic society for the protection of health".
The European Commission of Human Rights, which screens cases for the court, had concluded in an October 1995 report that the British justice system had not violated their human rights.

It found that the state could invade peoples' private lives in order to protect their safety, for example, to require them to wear a helmet while riding a motorcycle or to prevent them from committing suicide.
The decision was a welcome victory for Britain from a court accused by the conservative government of meddling in domestic affairs.

Britain's top law official, the Lord Chancellor, Lord Mackay of Clashfern, travelled to the court's headquarters in Strasbourg, eastern France, last November to urge it to rein in its enforcement of human rights rules and give greater weight to member states' national laws.
The rights commission angered London in September by agreeing to take up the case of a 12-year-old boy seeking to overturn British laws allowing his parents to smack him.
The court last year condemned Britain's system for jailing minors and in 1995 faulted it for the killings of three unarmed Irish Republican Army bombers in Gibraltar in 1988.
The court and the commission are part of the 40-nation Council of Europe, set up to foster democracy and human rights.
